questions.text: Waka music, a Yoruba popular genre historically performed predominantly by female Muslim vocalists and closely associated with artists such as Salawa Abeni, is best described as
options: an instrumental-only genre with no vocal content
a Western classical vocal form
an exclusively Christian liturgical genre
a vocal genre with Islamic devotional roots, typically accompanied by percussion
questions.explanation: Waka music is a Yoruba vocal genre rooted in Islamic devotional practice, historically associated with female singers such as Salawa Abeni, and typically accompanied by percussion instruments rather than melodic Western instruments.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: The agidigbo, a traditional Yoruba instrument prominent in Apala music, is best classified as
options: an aerophone, since it is blown like a horn
an idiophone (specifically a lamellophone), since its plucked metal or wooden tongues vibrate to produce pitch
a membranophone, since it has a stretched drumhead
a chordophone, since it uses tuned strings
questions.explanation: The agidigbo is a large lamellophone (a type of idiophone) with plucked tongues of metal or wood attached to a resonating box, producing pitched tones without any membrane, string, or air column being the primary sound source.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: The sekere, a beaded gourd rattle widely used in Yoruba traditional and popular music, is classified as
options: a chordophone
an aerophone
a membranophone
an idiophone
questions.explanation: The sekere produces sound through the vibration of its own solid gourd body and the beads striking its surface, making it a classic example of an idiophone rather than a drum, string, or wind instrument.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: The dundun ensemble, a family of variably-pitched hourglass 'talking' drums central to Yoruba traditional music, belongs to which instrument classification?
options: Idiophone
Aerophone
Membranophone
Chordophone
questions.explanation: The dundun family of hourglass-shaped talking drums produces sound through the vibration of a stretched membrane (skin), squeezed by cords under the player's arm to vary pitch, classifying them as membranophones.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: The bata drum ensemble, traditionally associated with Yoruba religious worship of the orisa Sango, is best classified as
options: a family of stringed chordophones
a set of double-headed, cone-shaped membranophones
a set of wind-blown aerophones
a family of struck metal idiophones only
questions.explanation: Bata drums are double-headed, cone-shaped membranophones traditionally used in Yoruba religious contexts, particularly in worship associated with the orisa Sango, and typically played in ensembles of varying sizes.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: The algaita, a reed wind instrument used in Hausa traditional and royal court music of northern Nigeria, is classified as
options: a chordophone
a membranophone
an idiophone
an aerophone
questions.explanation: The algaita is a double-reed wind instrument, related to the oboe, whose sound is produced by a vibrating column of air, classifying it as an aerophone.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: The goje, a traditional single-stringed bowed instrument found among the Hausa people, is classified as
options: an idiophone
an aerophone
a chordophone
a membranophone
questions.explanation: The goje is a traditional bowed lute with a single string stretched across a resonating body, and it is classified as a chordophone since its sound derives from the vibration of the string.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: The kakaki, a very long straight metal trumpet traditionally used in Hausa royal court ceremonies, produces sound through
options: the vibration of a stretched membrane at one end
the vibration of internal strings
the buzzing of the player's lips setting a column of air into vibration
the striking of its own metal body
questions.explanation: Like other trumpets, the kakaki produces sound when the player's buzzing lips excite the column of air within its long metal tube, classifying it as an aerophone (specifically a natural, valveless trumpet).

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: The balafon, a West African wooden-keyed percussion instrument fitted with gourd resonators beneath each key, is most accurately classified as
options: a chordophone, similar to the kora
a membranophone, similar to a drum
an aerophone, similar to a flute
an idiophone, a relative of the xylophone family
questions.explanation: The balafon is a member of the xylophone family, with tuned wooden bars struck to produce pitch and gourd resonators beneath amplifying the sound, making it an idiophone rather than a drum, string, or wind instrument.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: In the standard Western orchestral classification system (as opposed to the Hornbostel-Sachs system), instruments are generally grouped into which four families?
options: Strings, woodwind, brass, and percussion
Idiophones, aerophones, chordophones, and membranophones
Solo, chamber, choral, and orchestral
Major, minor, diminished, and augmented
questions.explanation: The conventional Western orchestral classification divides instruments into strings, woodwind, brass, and percussion, a system distinct from (though related to) the more universally applicable Hornbostel-Sachs scheme of idiophones, aerophones, chordophones, and membranophones.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Although commonly made of metal, the saxophone and modern flute are both classified within the orchestral woodwind family primarily because
options: they are always painted a particular colour
they were both invented before any brass instruments
they can only be played by seated orchestral musicians
their sound-producing mechanism (a vibrating reed for the saxophone, or an air stream split across an edge for the flute) follows the woodwind tradition, regardless of the material used to build them
questions.explanation: Orchestral family classification is based on how sound is produced rather than the instrument's material; the saxophone uses a single reed and the flute uses an air stream split across an edge, both woodwind mechanisms, despite frequently being constructed from metal.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Despite its name, the French horn belongs to the brass family rather than the woodwind family because its sound is produced by
options: the buzzing of the player's lips against a metal mouthpiece, exciting the air column within its tubing
a double reed vibrating in the mouthpiece
a vibrating string stretched across its body
a single reed similar to that of a clarinet
questions.explanation: The French horn is classified as brass because, like the trumpet and trombone, its tone is generated by the player's lips buzzing against a cup-shaped metal mouthpiece, exciting the air column, regardless of any 'horn' naming convention.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: The timpani (kettledrums), a staple of the Western orchestral percussion section, are distinctive among most drums because they
options: produce sound entirely without any membrane
can be tuned to specific, definite pitches, unlike most unpitched percussion instruments
are classified as chordophones due to internal strings
cannot be played as part of an orchestra
questions.explanation: Unlike most percussion instruments, which produce indefinite pitch, timpani can be tuned to specific pitches by adjusting the tension of their membrane, allowing them to fulfil distinct harmonic roles within orchestral writing.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Within orchestral percussion writing, instruments are commonly divided into 'pitched' and 'unpitched' categories; which of the following pairs correctly places one instrument in each category?
options: Snare drum (pitched); xylophone (unpitched)
Xylophone (pitched); snare drum (unpitched)
Triangle (pitched); glockenspiel (unpitched)
Bass drum (pitched); marimba (unpitched)
questions.explanation: The xylophone produces definite, tuned pitches and is therefore a pitched percussion instrument, while the snare drum produces indefinite pitch and is classified as unpitched percussion.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: The ogene, a hand-held metal bell used among the Igbo people (notably in highlife ensembles and traditional ceremonies), is classified as
options: an aerophone
a membranophone
an idiophone
a chordophone
questions.explanation: The ogene bell produces sound through the vibration of its own solid metal body when struck, making it an idiophone, distinct from drums, strings, or wind instruments.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Work songs, one important function of traditional African music, are primarily intended to
options: entertain paying audiences at formal concerts
accompany only funeral rites
coordinate the rhythm and pace of communal manual labour, such as farming or rowing
serve exclusively as lullabies for infants
questions.explanation: Work songs traditionally help synchronise and energise the rhythm of communal manual labour, such as farming, pounding, or rowing, illustrating music's practical social function beyond entertainment.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Dirges, another important category of traditional African vocal music, are specifically performed to
options: celebrate a marriage ceremony
accompany harvest festivals exclusively
mourn the dead and accompany funeral rites
coordinate manual labour tasks
questions.explanation: Dirges are mournful songs specifically associated with death and funeral rites, expressing grief and honouring the deceased within many African musical traditions.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Praise singing, a widespread tradition across many African societies (often performed by griots or similarly specialised musicians), primarily functions to
options: extol the virtues, lineage, and achievements of individuals, families, or rulers
criticise and mock important community leaders
accompany only children's games
provide purely instrumental background music with no vocal or textual content
questions.explanation: Praise singing traditionally celebrates and honours the achievements, lineage, and status of individuals, families, or rulers, often performed by specialised musicians such as griots who preserve genealogical and historical knowledge.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Which best distinguishes Highlife from Afrobeat in terms of typical musical emphasis?
options: Highlife has no melodic content whatsoever, while Afrobeat is purely melodic with no rhythm
Afrobeat originated centuries before Highlife
Highlife generally emphasises melodic dance band instrumentation, while Afrobeat emphasises extended jazz-funk-influenced grooves paired with socio-political lyrics
There is no meaningful musical difference between the two genres
questions.explanation: Highlife typically centres on melodic Western dance-band instrumentation (guitars, horns) with West African rhythmic sensibilities, while Afrobeat, pioneered by Fela Kuti, layers extended jazz- and funk-influenced grooves with pointed socio-political lyrical content.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: A heterophonic texture, occasionally found in traditional African ensemble performance, occurs when
options: multiple performers simultaneously play or sing slightly different, ornamented versions of essentially the same melody
a single unaccompanied melodic line is performed with absolutely no variation
only percussion instruments are permitted to perform
four independent, harmonically unrelated melodies are performed with no shared material
questions.explanation: Heterophony occurs when multiple performers render the same underlying melody simultaneously but with individual embellishments or slight variations, a texture found in various traditional musical practices, including some African ensemble performance.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: The cross-rhythm technique found extensively in West African drumming, in which two or more conflicting rhythmic groupings (such as a pattern in three against a pattern in two) occur simultaneously, is most precisely described as
options: monophony
a complete absence of rhythmic organisation
homophony
a specific and structured form of polyrhythm
questions.explanation: Cross-rhythm is a structured type of polyrhythm in which contrasting rhythmic groupings (for example, three-against-two) are deliberately superimposed, a technique fundamental to much West African drumming and its diasporic musical descendants.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Which of the following instrument groupings correctly places all three instruments within the same Hornbostel-Sachs classification?
options: Dundun, kakaki, and kora (all aerophones)
Sekere, ogene, and talking drum (all idiophones)
Balafon, algaita, and timpani (all membranophones)
Kora, goje, and violin (all chordophones)
questions.explanation: The kora, goje, and violin are all string instruments that generate sound through vibrating strings, correctly grouping them together as chordophones; the other listed groupings mix instruments from different classification categories.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: A half cadence, which many musicians treat as synonymous with an imperfect cadence, is best described as a progression that
options: ends on the tonic (I) chord in root position with the tonic note in the melody
moves from the subdominant directly to the tonic
moves from the dominant to the submediant
ends on the dominant (V) chord, leaving the phrase sounding harmonically unresolved
questions.explanation: A half cadence (often used interchangeably with 'imperfect cadence') ends on the dominant chord, creating a sense of pause or expectation rather than final resolution.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: A 'perfect authentic cadence', the strongest and most conclusive form of the V-I progression, additionally requires that
options: the dominant chord must appear in second inversion
the final tonic chord must include an added seventh
both chords appear in root position and the tonic note is present in the highest (melodic) voice at the final chord
the progression must be repeated exactly three times
questions.explanation: A perfect authentic cadence requires both the dominant and tonic chords to be in root position, with the tonic pitch sounding in the topmost voice of the final chord, distinguishing it from a merely 'imperfect' authentic cadence where these conditions are not fully met.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: The cadential six-four chord, a common device in Classical and Romantic harmony immediately preceding a cadence, is best understood as
options: a dominant seventh chord in root position
a plagal cadence in first inversion
an unrelated chromatic chord with no cadential function
a tonic chord in second inversion that functions harmonically as an embellishment of the dominant, typically resolving to a root-position dominant chord
questions.explanation: The cadential six-four is a tonic triad in second inversion (with the fifth in the bass) that, despite its tonic spelling, functions as a decorative prolongation of dominant harmony, typically resolving directly to a root-position V chord before the final tonic.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: A passing tone, a common type of non-chord (non-harmonic) tone, is best defined as a note that
options: is struck simultaneously with the chord tones and never resolves
must always be the root of the next chord
fills in the melodic space between two chord tones a third apart, moving stepwise and unaccented
can only occur in the bass voice
questions.explanation: A passing tone connects two chord tones a third apart by stepwise motion, typically falling on a weak beat, and does not belong to the underlying harmony of the moment.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: A suspension, a non-chord tone technique widely used in tonal harmony, is created by
options: sounding a note that leaps by a large interval with no preparation
eliminating a note from the texture entirely
preparing a chord tone in one harmony, holding it over (suspending it) as the harmony changes so it becomes dissonant, then resolving it down by step
playing all voices in strict parallel motion
questions.explanation: A suspension involves three stages: preparation (as a consonance), suspension (held over into a new harmony, becoming dissonant), and resolution (typically stepping down to a consonance), creating expressive harmonic tension.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: An appoggiatura, an ornamental non-chord tone often approached by leap and resolved by step, is generally distinguished from a passing tone by
options: typically occurring on a strong (accented) beat, creating an accented dissonance before resolving
always occurring only in unaccompanied solo music
never resolving to a chord tone
being approached and left by the same melodic interval
questions.explanation: Unlike the typically unaccented passing tone, an appoggiatura is usually placed on a strong beat, creating a pronounced accented dissonance that then resolves stepwise into the underlying harmony.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: A sequence, as a compositional device, refers to
options: a melodic or harmonic pattern immediately repeated at a different pitch level
a single note sustained indefinitely with no repetition
the exact repetition of a pattern at precisely the same pitch
a random, unrelated series of notes with no discernible pattern
questions.explanation: A sequence involves restating a melodic or harmonic pattern at a new pitch level (higher or lower), preserving its basic contour and intervallic relationships while providing a sense of forward motion.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: An ostinato, frequently found in both Western art music and traditional African drumming, refers to
options: a single note played only once at the very start of a piece
a rhythmic or melodic pattern that is persistently repeated, often underpinning other musical material above it
a technique for tuning an instrument
a term describing purely improvised, non-repetitive music
questions.explanation: An ostinato is a short musical pattern (melodic, rhythmic, or both) that is persistently repeated, often forming a foundational layer beneath other developing musical material.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: A trill, a common musical ornament, is executed by
options: playing two notes simultaneously and holding them
sliding continuously between two pitches with no distinct steps
rapidly alternating between a principal note and the note immediately above it
abruptly stopping a note before its full value is heard
questions.explanation: A trill is executed by rapidly alternating between a written principal note and the diatonic or chromatic note immediately above it, producing a shimmering ornamental effect.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: A mordent, another common musical ornament, is distinguished from a trill mainly by
options: consisting of only a single, brief alternation between the principal note and an adjacent note before returning, rather than sustained rapid alternation
requiring an entirely different instrument to perform
always being performed more slowly than a written whole note
never returning to the principal note
questions.explanation: Unlike a trill's sustained rapid alternation, a mordent consists of a single quick alternation between the principal note and an adjacent note (above or below), before returning promptly to the principal note.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: A tierce de Picardie (Picardy third) refers to the harmonic practice of
options: raising the second scale degree at a cadence
ending a piece or section in a minor key with a major tonic chord instead of the expected minor tonic chord
using only diminished chords throughout an entire piece
ending a major-key piece with a minor subdominant chord
questions.explanation: The Picardy third is the practice, common in Baroque and earlier music, of concluding a piece or section that is otherwise in a minor key with a major tonic chord, achieved by raising the minor third to a major third.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Modulation, as a harmonic process in tonal music, refers to
options: a change in the tempo of a piece with no harmonic implication
the exact repetition of a melody at the same pitch
a permanent, irreversible change in a piece's time signature only
a shift from one key to another within a piece, often facilitated by a pivot chord common to both keys
questions.explanation: Modulation describes the process of moving from one tonal centre (key) to another within a composition, frequently achieved smoothly through a pivot chord that functions diatonically in both the original and new keys.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: A secondary dominant, a common chromatic harmonic device in tonal music, is best described as
options: any chord that never resolves
a chord built exclusively from the notes of the tonic triad
a term describing a second, identical dominant chord played simultaneously with the first
a dominant-type chord that resolves not to the main tonic, but to a scale degree other than the tonic, temporarily 'tonicising' it
questions.explanation: A secondary dominant is a dominant-functioning chord (such as V of V) that temporarily resolves to and emphasises a scale degree other than the main tonic, briefly treating that degree as a local tonic.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Binary form, a common structural framework in Baroque instrumental music (particularly dance movements), is organised into
options: four contrasting, unrelated sections with no repetition
a single continuous section with no internal division
two main sections, often labelled A and B, each typically repeated
five sections arranged as a rondo
questions.explanation: Binary form divides a piece into two main sections (A and B), commonly each repeated, with the first section often modulating away from the tonic and the second returning to it.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Ternary form, another common structural framework, is organised into
options: three sections following an A-B-A pattern, in which the opening material returns after a contrasting middle section
two identical sections with no contrast
a single unbroken section
seven contrasting sections with no repetition
questions.explanation: Ternary form follows an A-B-A structure, presenting an opening section, a contrasting middle section, and then a return of the original material, providing both contrast and satisfying formal symmetry.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Rondo form, frequently used for the final movements of Classical-era symphonies and concertos, is characterised by
options: a single theme that never returns after its first statement
a recurring main theme (refrain) that alternates with contrasting episodes, such as A-B-A-C-A
purely improvised material with no fixed structure
exactly two sections repeated indefinitely
questions.explanation: Rondo form features a recurring principal theme (the refrain) that alternates with contrasting episodes, producing patterns such as A-B-A-C-A, commonly used in lively Classical-era finales.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Theme and variations form, used by composers such as Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven, involves
options: presenting an initial theme, followed by a series of sections that each transform or embellish that theme in a different way
a single, unchanging theme repeated identically many times with no alteration
a series of unrelated melodies with no shared thematic material
the complete absence of any melodic material
questions.explanation: Theme and variations form presents an initial melodic theme, followed by a sequence of variations that each alter the theme through changes in rhythm, harmony, texture, ornamentation, or mode, while retaining a recognisable link to the original.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Transposition, a common technique in music, refers to
options: shifting a passage of music to a different pitch level while preserving its intervallic relationships
changing only the dynamics of a passage
reversing the order of notes in a melody
altering the rhythm of a passage while keeping the pitches fixed
questions.explanation: Transposition moves a passage of music up or down to a new pitch level, preserving the exact pattern of intervals between notes, commonly used to accommodate different instrument ranges or vocal comfort.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: The term 'tessitura' refers to
options: the specific tempo marking indicated at the start of a piece
a type of cadence found only in choral music
the general pitch range in which a particular voice or instrumental part lies most comfortably and is used most often
the total duration of a musical work
questions.explanation: Tessitura describes the comfortable, most frequently used pitch range for a given voice or instrument within a piece, which may differ from its absolute outer range of possible notes.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: Word painting (or madrigalism), a technique especially prominent in Renaissance vocal music, refers to the practice of
options: musically illustrating the meaning of the text, such as setting the word 'ascending' to a rising melodic line
using purely instrumental music with no text at all
repeating the same note throughout an entire piece regardless of text
avoiding any connection between music and text meaning
questions.explanation: Word painting (madrigalism) involves shaping the music to reflect the literal meaning of the text being set, such as using a descending melodic line for words evoking falling or death, a technique especially favoured by Renaissance madrigal composers.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: In aural (ear-training) practice, a major triad heard in isolation is generally distinguished from a minor triad by its
options: identical sound in every respect, since major and minor triads cannot be distinguished by ear
brighter, more consonant and stable quality, compared to the minor triad's characteristically darker, more subdued quality
requirement of being played only on stringed instruments
having four notes instead of three
questions.explanation: Although both are built from stacked thirds, a major triad's major third above the root generally produces a brighter, more open quality, while a minor triad's minor third produces a comparatively darker, more subdued sound, a distinction ear-training exercises aim to sharpen.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: In aural interval recognition, a perfect fifth is often distinguished from a tritone (augmented fourth/diminished fifth) by
options: the perfect fifth's markedly consonant, stable quality, contrasted with the tritone's inherently dissonant and unstable, restless quality
the tritone's smoother, more consonant sound compared to the open, stable perfect fifth
having an identical number of semitones in both cases
the perfect fifth being impossible to hear on any instrument
questions.explanation: The perfect fifth (seven semitones) has a notably open, stable, consonant quality, whereas the tritone (six semitones) has a distinctly dissonant, unstable, and restless character, making the two intervals aurally quite distinguishable despite their close proximity in size.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: When practising chord-progression dictation, a I-IV-V-I progression in a major key is generally recognised by ear as
options: remaining on the tonic chord throughout with no harmonic movement
a progression that only occurs in minor keys
a progression consisting entirely of diminished chords
moving from tonic, to subdominant, to dominant, and back to tonic, producing a strong overall sense of harmonic departure and eventual resolution
questions.explanation: The I-IV-V-I progression is among the most fundamental in tonal harmony, moving from the stable tonic through the subdominant and dominant before returning home, and is widely used as a foundational aural-training example.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: A deceptive cadence used for aural analysis purposes is most easily recognised by ear because it
options: always sounds identical to a perfect authentic cadence
sets up the strong expectation of resolution to the tonic (via V) but instead resolves unexpectedly to another chord, typically the submediant
never involves the dominant chord at all
can only occur in compound time signatures
questions.explanation: A deceptive (interrupted) cadence is recognisable aurally because the dominant chord creates a strong expectation of resolving to the tonic, which is then subverted when the progression moves instead to an unexpected chord, most commonly the submediant.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: In rhythmic dictation exercises, a dotted rhythm (such as a dotted eighth note followed by a sixteenth note) is aurally distinguished from an even pair of eighth notes by its
options: identical, undifferentiated rhythmic feel
complete absence of any audible rhythm
requirement of a much slower overall tempo
distinctly uneven, 'long-short' rhythmic quality, as opposed to the even, balanced feel of two equal eighth notes
questions.explanation: A dotted rhythm produces a distinctly uneven 'long-short' effect, clearly differentiable by ear from the balanced, even quality of two equal eighth notes, an important distinction in rhythmic dictation training.

questions.subject: Music
questions.text: A plagal cadence is distinguished from a perfect (authentic) cadence mainly in that it
options: always sounds more harmonically unresolved than an imperfect cadence
can only be performed by a solo instrument, never a choir
moves from the subdominant (IV) to the tonic (I), rather than from the dominant (V) to the tonic (I)
requires the dominant seventh chord to be omitted entirely from the piece
questions.explanation: While a perfect cadence resolves from the dominant (V) to the tonic (I), a plagal cadence instead moves from the subdominant (IV) to the tonic (I), producing a gentler, still-conclusive close often heard as the 'Amen' at the end of hymns.
